Articles.subtitle: Notes on frontend development, React and the little things that make the web better.

items.title: React Performance Tips Every Developer Should Know
items.tagline: Simple, practical optimizations that make React apps feel snappier.
items.excerpt: From memoization to lazy loading — a practical checklist for keeping React apps fast without over-engineering.
content: React is fast by default, but real-world apps accumulate slow spots. The good news is that most performance issues come from a handful of common patterns.
Start by re-rendering less. Use memo() for heavy components, keep state as local as possible, and lift derived state into selectors where it makes sense.
Next, split your bundles. React.lazy and dynamic imports let users download only the code they need for the page they're on.
Finally, measure. Profile with React DevTools before optimizing so you fix real bottlenecks instead of guessing.

items.title: Responsive Layouts: Mobile-First Done Right
items.tagline: A practical guide to designing for every screen.
items.excerpt: Mobile-first isn't just a slogan. It's a workflow that produces simpler, faster and more flexible interfaces.
content: Designing mobile-first forces you to focus on the content that truly matters before adding enhancements for larger screens.
Use fluid units, flexible grids and modern CSS like grid and flexbox to let layouts adapt naturally instead of fighting with media queries everywhere.
Test on real devices early. Emulators help, but touch targets, font sizes and load time are best judged on actual hardware.
Remember that responsive design is also about performance — smaller screens often mean slower connections.

items.title: Modern CSS Tips That Save Real Development Time
items.tagline: Little-known tricks for cleaner, shorter stylesheets.
items.excerpt: Cascade layers, container queries and logical properties — modern CSS is quietly making frontend work much easier.
content: The modern CSS feature set has grown a lot: logical properties replace physical ones for effortless RTL support.
Container queries let components respond to their own width rather than the viewport, unlocking truly reusable cards and layouts.
Cascade layers give you predictable control over specificity, so overrides and design tokens are easier to manage.
Taken together, these features translate to less code, fewer bugs and faster feature work.

items.title: useEffect Patterns That Won't Bite You
items.tagline: A clear mental model for effects and dependencies.
items.excerpt: Effects run after render — understand when they fire, why they re-run, and how to keep them predictable.
content: useEffect runs after the browser paints, not during render. That timing matters: side effects belong here, while derived values belong in render or in lazy state initialization.
The dependency array is a contract, not a chore. Every value you read from the component scope should be listed, so your effect never reads stale data.
When a value changes often, consider whether the work belongs in an effect at all — event handlers and refs often keep logic simpler and closer to the user action.
And remember: effects are easy to start and easy to get wrong. A little discipline up front saves hours of head-scratching bugs.

items.title: CSS Grid vs Flexbox: When to Reach for Each
items.tagline: Two layout systems, two mental models — pick the right tool.
items.excerpt: Grid is for two-dimensional layouts, flexbox is for one. Here's a practical way to decide.
content: Ask one question first: does your layout flow in one direction or two? Letterbox containers and navs are often flexbox; entire pages and card walls are usually grid.
Grid excels at aligning rows AND columns, so gaps, tracks and placement become explicit and predictable.
Flexbox excels at distributing space within a single axis — wrapping chips, centering a button, stretching a footer.
The best pages use both. Start with grid for the page skeleton, then let flexbox arrange the pieces inside.

items.title: Building a Small Design System That Scales
items.tagline: Tokens, components and docs your team will actually use.
items.excerpt: You don't need a huge enterprise library — a small, disciplined system beats a sprawling one.
content: Start with tokens, not components. Colors, spacing, type and radii expressed once make every later decision consistent.
Build the boring primitives first: buttons, inputs, cards and headings that every screen depends on.
Document usage with real examples. A component without guidance gets misused; guidance without examples gets ignored.
Evolve it like software — review, refactor and version it, and your design system pays for itself within a few releases.
